questions.q: What are the three stages of ETL, in order?
options: Load, Transform, Extract
Extract, Transform, Load
Transform, Extract, Load
Extract, Load, Transform
questions.explain: Data is pulled out (Extract), cleaned and reshaped (Transform), then written to its destination (Load).

questions.q: What two real data-quality problems does orders.csv contain?
options: Duplicate order_id values and an invalid date format
A missing customer_name on one row and a negative quantity on another
Missing column headers and extra whitespace
A corrupted file encoding
questions.explain: Row 1005 is missing customer_name, and row 1014 has a quantity of -1.

questions.q: What is the orchestrator function's job in this lesson's pipeline design?
options: To contain all the cleaning logic directly
To call extract(), transform(), and load() in order, passing each output to the next
To open the database connection only
To replace the need for separate functions entirely
questions.explain: run_pipeline() wires the three stages together without containing their implementation details itself.

questions.q: Why does separating ETL into one function per stage make debugging easier?
options: It doesn't - a single combined function is just as easy to debug
Because Python requires at least three functions per script
Because each stage can be tested, logged, or replaced independently of the others
Because it reduces the file size
questions.explain: A bug can be isolated to one stage's function, instead of hunting through one large block of code.

questions.q: What does transform() do in this lesson's example pipeline?
options: Connects to a SQL Server database
Writes the DataFrame to a CSV file
Reads the raw CSV file into a DataFrame
Drops rows missing a customer_name and rows with a non-positive quantity
questions.explain: transform() applies the cleaning rules, using dropna() and a quantity filter.
